waste-reduction-s1.title: A city's trash before and after a pay-as-you-throw program

table.caption: Average household waste per week, in kilograms, one year before and one year after the city began charging by the bag (invented data for practice)

waste-reduction-s2.title: A passage on a plastic bag fee
waste-reduction-s2.passage: In 2020 a coastal city began charging shoppers 10 cents for each single-use plastic or paper bag at checkout. The mayor's office says the fee will cut litter on beaches and in storm drains and push shoppers to bring their own bags. A grocers' group opposes it, saying the fee is a hidden tax on low-income families and that reusable bags must be used many times before they are better for the environment than a thin plastic bag. One year later, the city reports that bags handed out at checkout fell by 70%, while sales of reusable bags rose. The grocers' group points out that sales of small plastic trash-can liners also rose.

items.q: Find the percent change in household trash sent to the landfill after the program began.

mistakes.why: You divided by the after value. Divide by the before value, 18.0 kg.
Landfill trash fell, so the change is negative: -35%.

items.q: Total household waste barely changed (23.0 to 22.0 kg). What does the program mainly do, based on the data?
options: It makes households produce far less waste overall
It shifts trash into recycling and compost
It moves waste from recycling into the trash
It has no effect on where waste goes

why.correct: Households moved material from the trash into recycling and compost, which are cheaper or free, so landfill trash fell much more than total waste.
options: Total waste fell by only 1 kg a week.
Right: recycling and compost rose as trash fell.
Recycling rose; it did not move into the trash.
Landfill trash fell 35%.

items.q: After the program, what percent of each household's total waste is diverted from the landfill by recycling and compost?

mistakes.why: That counts recycling alone. Add compost (3.8 kg) before dividing.
That is the landfill share (11.7 of 22.0). Diverted means recycling plus compost.

items.q: Is pay-as-you-throw a policy or a technology?
options: A policy: a city rule that charges by the bag
A technology: a machine that sorts recycling
A technology: special trash bags that break down
Neither: it is a natural change in habits

why.correct: Charging households by the bag of trash is a rule set by the city, so it is a policy. It works through a price incentive, not a device.
options: Right: it changes behavior with a price.
The program is a fee rule, not a machine.
The bags are not the point; the fee is.
The change followed the new fee rule.

items.q: What is the grocers' group's main claim?
options: The fee will cut litter on beaches
Bags handed out fell by 70%
Plastic bags should be banned outright
The fee is unfair and helps less than claimed

why.correct: The grocers argue that the fee is unfair to low-income families and may not help the environment as much as claimed.
options: That is the mayor's claim.
That is the city's report, not the grocers' claim.
The grocers oppose the fee; they do not call for a ban.
Right: fairness and doubtful benefit.

items.q: How does the rise in sales of plastic trash-can liners relate to the grocers' argument?
options: It proves the fee eliminated plastic use
It shows reusable bags break down faster
Some saved plastic came back as liners
It shows beaches have more litter than before

why.correct: People had reused checkout bags as trash liners; buying liners instead offsets part of the drop in plastic, which supports the grocers' doubt about the size of the benefit.
options: Liner sales rose, so plastic use did not vanish.
Liner sales say nothing about reusable bags breaking down.
Right: it weakens how much plastic was really saved.
The passage gives no litter data.

items.q: What assumption does the mayor's office make in predicting less beach litter?
options: Paper bags make up most beach litter
Checkout bags are a big share of litter
Reusable bags are seldom thrown away
Shoppers will stop buying groceries

why.correct: The prediction assumes that checkout bags are a meaningful share of beach and storm drain litter, so fewer bags handed out means less litter.
options: The mayor does not single out paper bags.
Right: the claim depends on bags being a real share of litter.
The mayor makes no claim about reusable bags lasting forever.
Nothing in the passage suggests that.

items.q: Order the waste hierarchy from most preferred to least preferred.
options: Reduce (make and use less)
Reuse (use things again)
Recycle and compost
Recover energy (waste-to-energy)
Dispose (landfill)

why.correct: Reducing avoids waste altogether; reusing keeps items in use; recycling and composting make new materials; energy recovery and landfilling are last.

items.q: Which action is an example of source reduction?
options: Using less packaging on products
Recycling aluminum cans into new cans
Burning trash to make electricity
Collecting methane from a landfill

why.correct: Source reduction means making less waste in the first place, such as designing products with less packaging or buying in bulk.
options: Right: less material is used, so less becomes waste.
Recycling handles waste after it is made.
That is energy recovery from waste.
That handles gas from waste already buried.

items.q: Why does recycling aluminum save so much energy compared with making new aluminum?
options: Recycled aluminum is lighter, so it is cheaper to ship
Recycling turns aluminum into a fuel
Recycled cans need no sorting or cleaning
It skips mining and refining ore

why.correct: Making new aluminum means mining bauxite ore and using huge amounts of electricity to separate the metal. Remelting used cans skips those steps and uses about 95% less energy.
options: Recycled and new aluminum weigh the same.
Aluminum is remelted into new metal, not burned.
Cans still need collecting and sorting.
Right: remelting cans takes about 5% of the energy.

items.q: Which is a drawback of recycling?
options: It increases the need for mining new ore
It adds methane to landfills
Collecting and sorting cost money
It makes products impossible to reuse

why.correct: Collecting, sorting and processing recyclables costs money and energy, and markets for some materials, especially mixed plastics, are weak, so some collected material is still landfilled.
options: Recycling reduces the need for new ore.
Recycling keeps material out of landfills.
Right: recycling is not free, and not all of it gets reused.
Recycling does not prevent reuse.

items.q: How does composting food scraps reduce methane from landfills?
options: Compost absorbs the methane the landfill makes
Food decays with oxygen, so less methane forms
Composting turns food into plastic
Composting burns food at high temperature

why.correct: In a compost pile, microbes break food down with oxygen, making CO2, water and humus. In a landfill, food breaks down without oxygen and makes methane.
options: Composting keeps food out of the landfill; it does not absorb landfill gas.
Right: aerobic decomposition makes CO2, not methane.
Composting makes humus-rich soil, not plastic.
Composting is decay, not burning.

items.q: Which choice is an example of reuse rather than recycling?
options: Refilling a glass milk bottle many times
Melting glass bottles into new jars
Shredding paper into pulp for new paper
Grinding plastic into flakes for fleece

why.correct: Refilling a glass bottle uses the same item again without breaking it down. Melting it into new glass would be recycling.
options: Right: the same bottle is used again.
Melting into new products is recycling.
Turning material into pulp is recycling.
Processing into new material is recycling.

items.q: Assume that recycling one aluminum can saves about 0.2 kWh of energy compared with making a new can from ore. A school recycles 12,000 cans a year. Write the setup for the kWh saved, then the answer.

mistakes.why: Multiply the number of cans by the kWh per can so cans cancel.
That is MWh. The question asks for kWh: 2,400.

items.q: A school sends most of its cafeteria food scraps to the landfill. Propose a solution, other than recycling, that reduces this waste, and explain how it works.

why.correct: It respects "other than recycling", fits a school, and says how it works: composting keeps food out of the landfill and makes soil.

specific.frame: The school could ___, which reduces landfill waste because ___.

action.label: Solution
options: compost the food scraps in a school garden
recycle the food containers
burn the scraps in the school boiler

why.1: The question says other than recycling, and the issue is food scraps.
why.2: Burning food at a school is unsafe and does not fit the setting.

how.label: How it works
options: microbes break the food down with oxygen into humus instead of making methane in a landfill
the scraps become plastic that can be reused
the scraps dry out and blow away

why.2: Scraps blowing away is litter, not a solution.

specific.model: The school could compost the food scraps in a school garden, which reduces landfill waste because microbes break the food down with oxygen into humus instead of making methane in a landfill.
